reasons: Type checking is turned off for the whole file.
Some debug routes expose configuration details to any logged-in user.
No tests are visible in this file.
The file is over three thousand lines, which makes changes harder to check.

terms.meaning: A web address the app answers, with code that runs when it is called.
A short-term memory of answers, so repeated requests are fast.
A check, done before the app runs, that each value has the expected kind.
A set of rules that checks the shape of incoming data before it is used.
Attach a group of routes or a module so the app answers its addresses.
The stage a project is in, such as under construction or operating.

used_by: Not visible in this packet; registerRoutes is exported for the server start-up code.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports for the whole route file
sections.what: Brings in the web framework, the data shape checker, storage, the login check, and the helper modules the routes use.
sections.why: The file gathers everything its routes need in one place.
sections.watch_out: Type checking is off, so a wrong import name may not be flagged until the route runs.

sections.name: param
sections.title: Reads a URL parameter safely
sections.what: Returns a named URL parameter as text, using empty text if it is missing. Also declares a flag that stops two maturity sweeps running at once.
sections.why: The flag comment says it stops concurrent triggers from piling up.
sections.watch_out: The flag is declared here but is not used in the sections shown, so check the rest of the file before relying on it.

sections.name: registerRoutes
sections.title: Entry point that attaches all routes
sections.what: The function the server calls to attach every route to the app. It returns the HTTP server.
sections.why: Likely reason: one place wires this route file into the app.
sections.watch_out: It waits for the tool modules to mount, so a failure there can stop the server from starting.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Login and sub-module attachment
sections.what: Attaches the login endpoint, then the portfolio, evidence and collation route groups, then mounts all tool modules under their own web addresses.
sections.why: The comments say adding a tool never needs an edit to this file.
sections.watch_out: The order matters: the groups are attached in this sequence, and tool modules are mounted last.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Admin data quality report
sections.what: Builds a data quality report for all projects, optionally for one industry, plus a readiness summary for the scan feature. Only admins may call it. If the data fetch is incomplete, it stops with an error rather than report partial data.
sections.why: The truncation check is written so that a partial report is never shown.
sections.watch_out: The fetch limit is 100000 projects, so a larger database triggers the truncation error.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Per-project cost and schedule data
sections.what: Returns the cost, schedule, capacity and status of projects in one industry, with the evidence behind each. Can be narrowed to a list of project IDs. Changes no data.
sections.why: The comment says this is the read-only foundation for the future Benchmark Scan feature.
sections.watch_out: Unknown IDs are skipped silently rather than reported.

sections.name: post
sections.title: AI summary of selected projects
sections.what: Asks the AI model to group the selected projects into what went wrong and what went right, without inventing facts. If the AI key is not set, it replies not_configured with status 200. If generation fails, it replies with 502.
sections.why: The comment says the key lives only on the server, and the slide should degrade gracefully when it is absent.
sections.watch_out: An empty ID list is refused, and if none of the IDs match, the reply is 404.

sections.name: get (part 1)
sections.title: Dashboard counts: start
sections.what: Starts building the home-page dashboard for one industry, optionally narrowed to chosen segments, using a cached answer when one exists. Counts projects by lifecycle stage and maps older stage names onto current ones. Defaults to the nuclear industry when none is given.
sections.why: The comments say the alias mapping keeps the counts right when older values exist, and that retired projects must not be folded into active stages.
sections.watch_out: Only the three named older values are mapped, so any other old stage name appears as its own bucket.

sections.name: get (part 2)
sections.title: Dashboard counts: capacity, budget and updates
sections.what: Counts projects by maturity, adds up reported megawatts (converting gigawatts), finds the budget range, and counts projects with a budget. Also fetches the twenty latest updates, leaving out bulk imports and ChatGPT research.
sections.why: The comment says only dimensions are normalised, not AC and DC, and that zero megawatts means unknown.
sections.watch_out: AC and DC figures are added together without conversion, so the total may not match a single plant rating, and zero megawatts is ignored rather than counted as zero.

sections.name: get (part 3)
sections.title: Dashboard counts: recent wins
sections.what: Collects approved project field edits from the last 30 days, leaving out bulk imports and value-layer made-current entries, and groups them by project into up to ten success stories.
sections.why: The code comments explain why value-layer entries are not project field edits.
sections.watch_out: Only the newest 50 changes are read, so a busy project can push older wins out of the list.

sections.name: get (part 4)
sections.title: Dashboard counts: caching and reply
sections.what: Stores the dashboard answer in the cache for the dashboard time to live, then sends it. On error returns a 500 with generic text.
sections.why: Likely reason: avoids repeating heavy database work on every page view. Not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The cache key holds only the industry and segments, so a fresh import may not appear until the cache expires.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Shows which search and model providers are available
sections.what: Reports which search providers and model providers are available, plus the model router's configuration, for logged-in users.
sections.why: Likely reason: a debugging aid for missing providers. The name suggests this, but the code does not state it.
sections.watch_out: It shows the model router configuration to any logged-in user, so treat it as internal information.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Shows which AI key is set and part of its value
sections.what: Reports whether an OpenAI or OpenRouter key is set, which key name was found, and the first six characters of the OpenAI key. Also says whether the LLM extractor or a stub extractor is active.
sections.why: Likely reason: to diagnose why extraction falls back to the stub. Not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Any logged-in user receives the first six characters of the OpenAI key, which is a partial secret. Remove the prefix or restrict this route.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Counts projects per segment
sections.what: For one industry, counts projects in each segment card, including projects in child segments. The total also includes projects with a blank segment. Results are cached for the project list time to live.
sections.why: The comment says the total must match the Explore total shown elsewhere.
sections.watch_out: Projects with a blank segment count toward the total but appear in no card, so a user may think they are missing. A warning is logged when this happens.

sections.name: get (part 1)
sections.title: Project list filters and cache check
sections.what: Reads the search and filter options from the web address, checks they are valid, and sends back a saved result if the same request was made recently. Unless the request says otherwise, the list shows only nuclear projects.
sections.why: Likely reason: repeated list requests are common, so a saved copy avoids repeating database work. The nuclear default is explained in the code comment for legacy pages.
sections.watch_out: The cache key is built from the filters, so any new filter must be added to the key or different requests will receive the same saved result.

sections.name: get (part 2)
sections.title: Loads projects and builds list response
sections.what: Fetches the matching projects, optionally attaches evidence to each row, wraps the rows with a total and paging values, saves the response in the cache, and sends it.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the comment that evidence is opt-in so existing consumers keep the same response.
sections.watch_out: The response reports a page size of 50 when no limit is given, but the database call may use its own default, so the reported page size could be wrong.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Lists recent project updates with paging
sections.what: Returns a page of project update items, each with its date, headline, source and link. The page size is kept between 1 and 100, and the list can be limited to one industry.
sections.why: Likely reason: the updates feed is paged so the screen does not load every update at once.
sections.watch_out: This response is saved using the project detail cache time rather than a list time, so its freshness depends on that setting.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Returns full details for one project
sections.what: Returns all details for one project. Admins also see how many proposed changes are waiting for review. A missing project returns a not found error.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code for the cache, though the admin-only review count is visible in the code.
sections.watch_out: Details are saved per role, so a change that does not clear the project cache will show old details for up to the cache time.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Source quotes behind a project's facts
sections.what: Returns the active source quotes for a project, grouped by field. If a field path is given, it returns only the quotes for those fields, with duplicates removed.
sections.why: The code comment says list pages show shortened quotes, and this endpoint supplies the full text when a user opens a citation.
sections.watch_out: Quote removal of duplicates is done only within one response, so the same quote can still appear under different fields.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Full output of scan runs for a project
sections.what: Lists every scan run that included the project, along with each candidate source, its values, calculations, reasons and gaps. Each record gets a citation id so the source drawer can open it.
sections.why: The code comment says the complete output of each run is needed, including sources that were held back.
sections.watch_out: This GET request writes new research source records when a citation is missing, so repeated calls add database writes.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Lessons Learnt use of a project
sections.what: Shows the Lessons Learnt runs that used this project, with each run's status, acceptance state and scope, plus each item's route, category and the slides where it appears.
sections.why: The code comment says the data is written by a separate run stage and this endpoint only reads it.
sections.watch_out: The database queries are written as raw SQL, so renaming a table or column would break this endpoint without any other warning.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Text and location of one evidence item
sections.what: Returns the verbatim text, link, publisher and date for one evidence item, plus a location hint such as a text fragment, PDF page or anchor. Ids starting with rs- are looked up in a separate research store.
sections.why: Likely reason: research sources and internal evidence are stored separately, so the id prefix decides where to look.
sections.watch_out: Every failure, including database errors, is returned as a generic could not be retrieved message with no log entry, which hides the real cause.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Snapshot status and capture for evidence
sections.what: Returns the status of the saved screenshot for one evidence item and captures one on the first request. A retry flag asks for another attempt. Items with no source link get a no URL status.
sections.why: The code comment says the first request captures on demand, and failed captures are stored so dead links are not retried on every open.
sections.watch_out: The first capture can take 5 to 30 seconds, and using the retry flag repeatedly will trigger repeated captures.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Streams the saved snapshot picture
sections.what: Sends the stored PNG screenshot for one evidence item. It never takes a new screenshot and returns not found when no image is stored or the file is missing.
sections.why: The code comment says only the metadata endpoint may capture, so this endpoint is read only.
sections.watch_out: The image is marked to be cached in the browser for an hour, so a newly captured image may not appear for up to an hour. A failure during streaming cannot send a normal error message.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Glossary terms for an industry
sections.what: Returns the glossary terms for one industry, defaulting to nuclear, and saves the result in the cache.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code for the cache, though it is a common way to avoid repeated reads.
sections.watch_out: If the glossary cache time is set to zero, the code falls back to one hour instead of turning caching off.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Change history for one project
sections.what: Returns the change log entries for a project, optionally for a single field, with paging controls.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The endpoint simply exposes the change log for review.
sections.watch_out: The paging values come straight from the web address and are not checked, so text that is not a number is passed on to the database query.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Latest changes across all projects
sections.what: Returns the most recent change log entries, by default the latest 20, optionally limited to one industry.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. It gives a quick overview of recent edits.
sections.watch_out: The limit has no upper bound, so a very large number could return a large response.

sections.name: get (part 1)
sections.title: Latest change and pending review for a field
sections.what: Returns the latest change to one field of a project. Admins also see that change if it is still waiting for review.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the admin-only review visibility.
sections.watch_out: Non-admin users always get no pending change, which can look the same as having nothing waiting when a review is actually pending.

sections.name: get (part 2)
sections.title: Rules for which project fields can be edited
sections.what: Lists the project fields that can be edited and the type each must have. Any other field in an edit request is refused.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code, though the strict check is visible and it blocks unknown fields from being saved.
sections.watch_out: When a new project field is added to the database, it must also be added here, or edits to that field will be refused.

sections.name: patch
sections.title: Admin edits a project and logs changes
sections.what: Lets an admin change project fields. Each field that really changes is first written to the change log as approved, then the project is saved. This section also defines the rules for technology details used in the next section.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeping a log of every manual edit gives an audit trail of who changed what.
sections.watch_out: The log entries and the project update are separate database writes with no shared transaction, so a failure between them can leave the history out of step with the project.

sections.name: patch
sections.title: Admin edits technology details
sections.what: Lets an admin change the technology details of a project. Each changed field is logged under the technology heading, and the details are created if they do not yet exist.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the logging pattern shared with other edits.
sections.watch_out: When no technology record exists yet, the old values are treated as empty, so the log will show every entered field as a new value.

sections.name: patch
sections.title: Admin edits one scorecard pillar
sections.what: Lets an admin change the score, trend, confidence, strengths and weaknesses of one scorecard pillar. Each change is logged, and the pillar must belong to the project named in the address.
sections.why: The code checks that the pillar belongs to the project, which prevents editing another project's scorecard through a mismatched address.
sections.watch_out: The ownership check is the only protection against editing a pillar from another project, so removing it would open that gap.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Adds a milestone to a project
sections.what: Creates a new milestone for a project with a name, planned and actual dates, and a status. The creation is written to the change log.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the change log pattern used for other new records.
sections.watch_out: The old value for a new milestone is logged as the text null, which is different from how the edit paths record old values.

sections.name: patch (part 1)
sections.title: Edits one milestone of a project
sections.what: Lets an admin change a milestone's name, dates or status. Each change is logged, and the milestone must belong to the project in the address. This section also defines the rules for a source location, which must be a text fragment, PDF page or anchor, with a 2000 character limit.
sections.why: The ownership check stops a milestone from one project being edited through another project's address.
sections.watch_out: The source location rules are defined here but used in the update routes below, so changing them affects those routes too.

sections.name: patch (part 2)
sections.title: Rules for adding project updates
sections.what: Sets the rules for a new project update: the date must be written as year, month, day, the headline and source are required with length limits, and the link, quote and location are optional. Extra fields are refused.
sections.why: The strict rules keep incoming update data to a known shape.
sections.watch_out: The date rule checks only the pattern, so a date such as one with an impossible month or day still passes.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Adds a dated update to a project
sections.what: Creates a dated news-style update for a project, logs the creation, and clears the saved project and update lists so the new item appears.
sections.why: Clearing the saved lists ensures the new update is visible immediately rather than after the cache expires.
sections.watch_out: The date is saved as entered once it matches the pattern, so an invalid calendar date will be stored.

sections.name: patch
sections.title: Edits the link of a project update
sections.what: Lets an admin change only the link of an existing update. The change is logged when the link really changes, and the saved lists are cleared.
sections.why: The code limits edits to the link, so other facts of an update stay as first recorded.
sections.watch_out: The link is checked only for length, not for whether it is a valid web address.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Adds an issue to a project
sections.what: Creates an issue for a project with a lifecycle stage, an impact level of low, medium, high or critical, a description and optional evidence references. The creation is logged.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the fixed impact levels, which keep the data consistent.
sections.watch_out: Evidence references are accepted as plain text and are not checked against real evidence records.

sections.name: patch
sections.title: Edits an issue of a project
sections.what: Lets an admin change the impact, description or evidence references of one issue. Each change is logged, and the issue must belong to the project.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The ownership check matches the pattern used for other sub-records.
sections.watch_out: The lifecycle stage cannot be changed here, so a wrong stage must be fixed some other way.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Adds a glossary term
sections.what: Creates a glossary term with its definition, an industry that defaults to nuclear, and optional citations. The glossary cache is cleared afterwards.
sections.why: Clearing the glossary cache lets the new term show immediately.
sections.watch_out: The format of citations is defined in a separate schema that is not visible here, so the exact accepted shape is unclear from this section.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Admin approves a pending change
sections.what: Marks a pending change as approved. If the change is for a top-level project field, the new value is copied onto the project, and the approval is logged.
sections.why: Likely reason: changes proposed by automated processes wait for review, and approval applies them.
sections.watch_out: If the new value is not valid JSON, it is saved as raw text without any error, so a bad value can be written silently.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Admin rejects a pending change
sections.what: Marks a pending change as rejected and logs the rejection. Only changes still waiting for review can be rejected.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the review state check.
sections.watch_out: Whether the rejected value was ever applied to the project is not visible in this section, so confirm before assuming the project is unchanged.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Starts a research job for a project
sections.what: Starts a background research job for one project. It is refused when a job is already running or when a job finished within the cooldown period, which defaults to five minutes and is set by an environment variable. Admins and analysts can use it.
sections.why: The cooldown limits how often one project can be researched, which controls cost and load. The code comment does not state a reason beyond this.
sections.watch_out: The cooldown setting is read when the server starts, so a change needs a restart, and two requests sent close together can both pass the check before either job is recorded.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Maturity tier and gates for a project
sections.what: Returns a project's maturity tier, whether it has been researched, its gate results and the full maturity framework.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the visible tier calculation from the gates.
sections.watch_out: A project counts as researched if any gate is not unknown, so a single partial result marks the whole project as researched.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Runs maturity research for one project now
sections.what: Runs maturity research for one project inside the request, then clears the dashboard cache and returns the result.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Running it directly gives the caller the result in one step.
sections.watch_out: Because the work runs inside the web request, slow research can make the caller time out even though the work continues.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Starts a maturity sweep over many projects
sections.what: Starts background maturity research across up to a chosen number of projects, using one to four workers at a time. It refuses to start if a sweep is already running and replies right away with an accepted status.
sections.why: Likely reason: a sweep over many projects is slow, so it runs in the background and only one sweep runs at a time.
sections.watch_out: The running flag is kept only in memory, so a server restart clears it and a new sweep can start while an older one is still in progress.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Latest research job and its steps
sections.what: Returns the newest research job for a project and the status and any error of each of its steps. The final output is included only for the commit step.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. It lets the screen show progress of the most recent job.
sections.watch_out: The code assumes the job list is sorted newest first, so a change in that sort order would show the wrong job.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Past research jobs for a project
sections.what: Returns all research jobs for a project, and optionally each job's steps.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the optional steps flag, which avoids extra work when only the list is needed.
sections.watch_out: Including steps makes one extra database call per job, which can be slow for projects with many jobs.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Cancels the active research job
sections.what: Marks the currently active research job as cancelled and records the time it ended.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. It gives users a way to stop a job they no longer need.
sections.watch_out: This only changes the status record, and whether the running work actually stops is not visible in this section.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Research documents for a project or job
sections.what: Returns the documents gathered by research. If a job id is given, it returns that job's documents; otherwise it returns up to 100 documents for the project.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the job filter.
sections.watch_out: The project view is capped at 100 documents with no paging, so older documents are not shown.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Projects with the most missing data
sections.what: Checks up to 500 projects for blank key fields, such as budget, owner and dates, and returns up to the chosen number with at least one gap, worst first. A zero counts as missing except for delay months.
sections.why: Likely reason: it helps the team choose which projects to fill in next.
sections.watch_out: Only the first 500 projects are checked, so projects beyond that are never suggested.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Starts an enrichment batch in background
sections.what: Checks the batch options and replies at once that the enrichment has started. The batch then runs in the background and logs a summary when it finishes.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the immediate reply, which avoids a long wait for the admin.
sections.watch_out: The reply says started even if the batch later fails, and the failure appears only in the server log.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Runs an enrichment batch and waits
sections.what: Checks the batch options, runs the enrichment, and returns the full report when it finishes.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. It is useful for small batches where the caller wants the result immediately.
sections.watch_out: The caller waits for the whole batch, so large batches may time out before a response is sent.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Map points for projects without location
sections.what: For each project without coordinates whose country is known, sets a point at the country's centre with a small random offset. It counts the projects updated, skipped and unresolved.
sections.why: Likely reason: projects need coordinates to appear on the map, and country centres are a rough fallback when exact locations are missing.
sections.watch_out: The random offset means the points can move on each run, and the project cache is not cleared, so the map may show old positions until the cache expires.

sections.name: post (part 1)
sections.title: Queues research jobs for many projects
sections.what: Chooses up to a chosen number of projects, skipping those already researched unless forced, and queues a research job for each one that has no active job. It also defines the shape of data accepted for file imports and sets a 5 MB size limit.
sections.why: Likely reason: queuing many jobs at once lets an admin start a large research pass in one action.
sections.watch_out: Only the first 500 projects are considered, and the jobs are only queued here, so whether they run depends on a runner that is not visible in this section.

sections.name: post (part 2)
sections.title: Checks file import data before use
sections.what: Checks an import request by confirming the industry is known and the data is under the size limit. If a check fails, it sends an error and stops.
sections.why: Likely reason: the checks protect the import from unknown industries and very large uploads.
sections.watch_out: The size is measured on the text form of the records, so it is close to but not exactly the size of the upload.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Previews a file import without saving
sections.what: Runs a file import in preview mode and returns the plan of what would change. Nothing is saved.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the dry run flag. A preview lets an admin check the plan before committing.
sections.watch_out: A preview cannot confirm that the save step itself will succeed.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Saves a file import to the database
sections.what: Runs a file import for real and records which admin started it. The result is returned to the caller.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the admin requirement and the recorded user.
sections.watch_out: Nothing in this section undoes a partial import if it fails midway, and how failures are handled is not visible here.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Lists all project schedules with names
sections.what: Returns every project schedule along with the project's name, or Unknown when the project cannot be found.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The names make the list readable for admins.
sections.watch_out: Each project is looked up one at a time, which can be slow when there are many schedules.

sections.name: put
sections.title: Sets a project's repeat schedule
sections.what: Saves a repeating schedule for a project. It checks the repeat rule and time zone, works out the next run time, and saves the result.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the validation steps.
sections.watch_out: The next run time is set using the UTC clock with the chosen hour and minute, so the chosen time zone is not applied to that run time.

sections.name: delete
sections.title: Turns off a project's schedule
sections.what: Disables a project's schedule so it stops running. The schedule record is kept.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Disabling rather than deleting keeps the history.
sections.watch_out: The route name says delete, but the schedule is only switched off, not removed.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Adds a company record
sections.what: Creates a company with a name, a type from a fixed list, and optional country, website and description.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the fixed list of company types, which keeps the data consistent.
sections.watch_out: New company types must be added to the fixed list in code, so they cannot be used until the code changes.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Lists companies with source and project counts
sections.what: Returns all companies, optionally limited to one industry, with the number of sources and linked projects each has.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The counts give a quick view of how well each company is covered.
sections.watch_out: Two separate lookups run for each company, so large lists can be slow to load.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Company pack list with counts
sections.what: Serves the list of ready-made company packs for an industry. For each pack it shows how many companies it holds, how many are not yet in the database, and how many already are.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets an admin see what a pack would add before importing it.
sections.watch_out: Matching uses both company name and web domain, so two companies that share a domain are treated as the same company.

sections.name: post (part 1)
sections.title: Start importing a company pack
sections.what: Admin request that loads one company pack for an industry and prepares it for import. It rejects bad input and returns not found when the pack id does not exist.
sections.why: Likely reason: checks the input before any database work starts.
sections.watch_out: The industry defaults to nuclear when it is not sent, so a missing industry field quietly imports into that industry.

sections.name: post (part 2)
sections.title: Create companies and their aliases
sections.what: Walks through each company in the pack. Existing companies only receive new aliases and are counted as duplicates. New companies are created with their name and website, plus alias entries, and the totals are returned.
sections.why: Likely reason: avoids creating the same company twice when a pack is imported again.
sections.watch_out: Each alias save is wrapped in a silent catch, so a failed alias is skipped without any message in the response.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Company detail with links and aliases
sections.what: Returns one company with its sources, the projects it is linked to (with project names), and its alternate names. Unknown companies get a not found reply.
sections.why: Likely reason: one request gives the company page everything it needs.
sections.watch_out: A linked project that no longer exists is shown as Unknown rather than hidden.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Add a source to a company
sections.what: Adds a source link (website, newsroom, investor page, feed, or PDF) to a company after checking that the company exists and the input is valid.
sections.why: Likely reason: the allowed source types are fixed, so bad types are rejected before saving.
sections.watch_out: The source type list here is separate from the list used by bulk imports, so the two can drift apart.

sections.name: patch
sections.title: Update one company source
sections.what: Changes whether a company source is enabled, its web address, or its notes. Fields that are not sent are left alone.
sections.why: Likely reason: a partial update lets a screen change one field at a time.
sections.watch_out: The web address check relies on truthiness, so an empty string is ignored instead of being rejected.

sections.name: delete
sections.title: Delete one company source
sections.what: Removes a source from a company and replies with no content on success.
sections.why: Likely reason: a successful delete has nothing to send back.
sections.watch_out: The company id in the path is not checked, so any source id can be deleted through any company's path.

sections.name: post (part 1)
sections.title: Start a discovery job in background
sections.what: Starts a search for new projects as a background job and returns right away with a job id. It refuses if a job is already running or if the last one finished too recently.
sections.why: Likely reason: a discovery run can take a long time, so the request does not wait for it to finish.
sections.watch_out: The running-job check and the job creation are not locked together, so two requests sent at the same moment could both start a job.

sections.name: post (part 2)
sections.title: Reply with queued job id
sections.what: Sends the new job id and a queued status back to the caller. This is the end of the start-job handler and runs only if the job was created without error.
sections.why: Likely reason: the caller gets an answer quickly while the work continues in the background.
sections.watch_out: The caller sees success before the job has run, so a failed job only shows up in the status endpoints.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Latest or specific discovery job status
sections.what: Returns one discovery job, either the one named in the query or the most recent one. Returns null when there is no job.
sections.why: Likely reason: an admin screen can poll this to show progress.
sections.watch_out: Returns a null job rather than an error when no job exists, so the screen must handle null.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Last twenty discovery jobs
sections.what: Returns the twenty most recent discovery jobs for the history view.
sections.why: Likely reason: a fixed limit keeps the history response small.
sections.watch_out: The limit of twenty is fixed in the code, so older jobs cannot be reached from this endpoint.

sections.name: get
sections.title: List sources with filters
sections.what: Returns sources, optionally filtered by type, enabled state, and industry.
sections.why: Likely reason: admin screens need to narrow long source lists.
sections.watch_out: Any enabled value other than the exact text true or false is treated as no filter.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Create one new source
sections.what: Adds a single source with a required id, name, type, web address, and authority tier from 1 to 5 (default 3).
sections.why: Likely reason: checks the input shape before saving.
sections.watch_out: The caller chooses the id, so duplicate ids are rejected only if the database enforces uniqueness.

sections.name: patch
sections.title: Update one source
sections.what: Changes the name, type, address, authority tier, category, region, or enabled flag of an existing source. Returns not found if the id does not exist.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Category and region accept an explicit null to clear them, while the other fields do not.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Return wind register data
sections.what: Sends the stored wind register to any signed-in user.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The data comes from windRegister, which is defined outside this excerpt.
sections.watch_out: Unlike most routes here, this one is open to any signed-in user, not only admins.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Source pack list with counts
sections.what: Lists the source packs for an industry, with how many sources each holds, how many are new, and how many are already present by web domain.
sections.why: Likely reason: same preview purpose as the company pack list.
sections.watch_out: A source with a web address that cannot be parsed is counted as new, which can overstate what an import would add.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Import a source pack
sections.what: Adds the sources from one pack for an industry, skipping any whose web domain already exists, and reports the counts and per-source results.
sections.why: Likely reason: matching by domain stops the same publisher from being added twice.
sections.watch_out: Source saves are not wrapped one by one, so an error partway through stops the import with earlier sources already saved.

sections.name: get
sections.title: List sources linked to a project
sections.what: Returns the sources attached to one project.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Only sign-in is checked, so any signed-in user can read any project's sources.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Attach a source to a project
sections.what: Links an existing source to a project by id and replies with ok.
sections.why: Likely reason: a link table connects projects and sources, so the link is added rather than copied.
sections.watch_out: Whether a repeat link is harmlessly ignored depends on storage behavior that is not shown here.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Companies on a project grouped by role
sections.what: Returns the companies linked to a project, plus the same list sorted into groups by role. Companies without a role go under UNKNOWN.
sections.why: Likely reason: the project page shows one section per role.
sections.watch_out: Grouping uses the role as stored, so a misspelled role creates its own group.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Link a company to a project
sections.what: Adds or updates a company's role on a project, records the change in the change log as approved, and clears cached project data.
sections.why: Likely reason: a log entry gives a manual change the same trail as automated ones.
sections.watch_out: The old value is always written as the text null, even when a link already existed, so the log can misstate the prior state.

sections.name: patch
sections.title: Update company details
sections.what: Changes a company's name, type, country, website, description, headquarters, or founding year. Returns not found when the company does not exist.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The name is limited to 200 characters, but the type and founding year have no such limit.

sections.name: get
sections.title: Projects linked to a company
sections.what: Returns the projects a company is linked to, plus the same list grouped by role.
sections.why: Likely reason: mirrors the project-side company view.
sections.watch_out: Missing roles are grouped under UNKNOWN, which can hide incomplete data.

sections.name: get
sections.title: List a company's alternate names
sections.what: Returns the alias names stored for one company.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The company is not checked to exist, so an unknown id returns an empty list instead of not found.

sections.name: post
sections.title: Add an alternate name to a company
sections.what: Stores a new alias for an existing company. The source defaults to MANUAL.
sections.why: Likely reason: aliases let later imports match the same company under another name.
sections.watch_out: There is no check for duplicate alias text, so the same alias can be stored twice.

sections.name: delete
sections.title: Delete a company alias
sections.what: Removes one alias by its id and replies ok.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The company id in the path is not checked against the alias, so any alias can be removed through any company's path.

sections.name: post (part 1)
sections.title: Bulk import: match projects by name
sections.what: Starts a bulk import for many projects at once. For each project it looks for an exact name match, then a loose name match, and records the project as not found or ambiguous when needed.
sections.why: Likely reason: research output often uses slightly different project names.
sections.watch_out: The loose match turns hyphens and spaces into wildcards, so a short name can match several projects and is then reported as ambiguous instead of imported.

sections.name: post (part 2)
sections.title: Bulk import: fill empty fields
sections.what: For each matched project, fills only the fields that are currently empty and logs each change as approved. Fields that already have a value are listed as skipped.
sections.why: Likely reason: prevents overwriting data someone has already reviewed.
sections.watch_out: A budget value is also copied into the planned budget when that is empty, so one incoming value changes two fields.

sections.name: post (part 3)
sections.title: Bulk import: save quotes and updates
sections.what: For each filled field that has a quote and a web address, saves the quote and a matching project update. Then adds listed sources that are not already known.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the evidence trail for each value that was filled in.
sections.watch_out: Quote and update saves are wrapped in silent catches, so a failed save leaves no trace in the response.

sections.name: post (part 4)
sections.title: Bulk import: save new sources and dry run
sections.what: Adds each new source row. In dry-run mode the same steps only report what would change and write nothing.
sections.why: Likely reason: dry run lets a user preview the import safely.
sections.watch_out: The duplicate source check matches any stored address that contains the host name, so a close but different address can block a real source.

sections.name: post (part 1)
sections.title: Research pack endpoint setup and schema
sections.what: Accepts one full research pack for a project in a single request. Only admins and analysts can call it, and the project must already exist. This part sets up the start of the expected shape for project fields.
sections.why: Likely reason: one request keeps related research changes together.
sections.watch_out: Fields the schema does not list are dropped silently, so a new field must be added here before it can be saved.

sections.name: post (part 2)
sections.title: Research pack schema: sources, quotes, updates
sections.what: Defines the expected shape of the sources, evidence quotes, dated updates, companies, milestones, and issues in a research pack.
sections.why: Likely reason: checks each list before any write begins.
sections.watch_out: Source authority must be between 1 and 3 here, while the separate source endpoint allows 1 to 5.

sections.name: post (part 3)
sections.title: Research pack schema: scorecard and technology
sections.what: Defines the expected shape of scorecard pillars, sku mappings, technology detail, and the success story.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the scoring fields consistent with what the database stores.
sections.watch_out: Scores must be 0 to 5 and alignment must be 0 to 100, so one out-of-range value fails the whole pack.

sections.name: post (part 4)
sections.title: Research pack: project fields and sources
sections.what: Opens one database transaction for the whole pack, then writes the project fields and links each source, creating it when new.
sections.why: Likely reason: one transaction means a failure rolls back everything in the pack.
sections.watch_out: Project fields are written as sent, so an empty string in a field overwrites the stored value.

sections.name: post (part 5)
sections.title: Research pack: companies and links
sections.what: Finds each company by name or alias, creating it if missing, fills in a blank website or type, then adds or updates its link to the project for that role.
sections.why: Likely reason: one company can hold several roles on the same project.
sections.watch_out: Company names are matched with a pattern that treats percent and underscore characters as wildcards, so unusual names can match the wrong company.

sections.name: post (part 6)
sections.title: Research pack: replace quotes, milestones, updates
sections.what: Replaces the stored evidence quotes and milestones with the pack's versions. Adds project updates only when the date and headline are new.
sections.why: Likely reason: replacing keeps repeated imports from piling up duplicate rows.
sections.watch_out: Sending an empty list for quotes or milestones deletes all stored ones, because only a section left out of the pack is skipped.

sections.name: post (part 7)
sections.title: Research pack: replace issues, scores, skus, story
sections.what: Replaces the issues, scorecard pillars, sku mappings, and success story for the project, and creates or updates the technology detail row.
sections.why: Likely reason: same replace approach as the earlier sections.
sections.watch_out: A section left out of the pack is kept, but a section sent as an empty list clears what was stored.

sections.name: post (part 8)
sections.title: Finish research pack and report counts
sections.what: After the transaction succeeds, clears cached project data and returns the counts of what changed. On error it returns a server error with the message.
sections.why: Likely reason: cached views would otherwise keep showing old values.
sections.watch_out: The error reply includes the raw error message, which may reveal internal detail to the caller.

summary: The main route file: it attaches many of the app's web routes, including login, the admin data quality report, scan data, the dashboard home, and segment counts.
purpose: Connects web addresses such as the dashboard home, scan data and segment counts to the code that answers them.
why: The file header says it is a large legacy route file being ported, which is why type checking is switched off for it.
how: First it sets up imports. Then registerRoutes attaches the login route, the portfolio, evidence and collation groups, and mounts tool modules. Each route then checks input, reads from the database or a helper, and returns JSON. Dashboard results are cached for a short time.
inputs: HTTP requests with URL parameters, query strings and JSON bodies; the database; the cache; the model and search providers; the logged-in user's role.
outputs: JSON responses. Scan synthesis returns a status and the AI-written themes, or not_configured when the AI key is absent.
risks: Type checking is switched off for the whole file, so type errors are hidden. A debug route shows the first six characters of the OpenAI key to any logged-in user. Only part of the file is in this packet, so this note covers only those sections.
debug: Find a route by its web address using the outline. Check the server error lines named in each catch block. For dashboard data, a stale result may come from the cache. For scan synthesis, not_configured means the AI key is missing on the server.
